The Utah roundmouth snail (Valvata utahensis) is a small operculate gastropod endemic to freshwater habitats of the Great Basin. Newly hatched individuals emerge from egg capsules with a shell height of only 0.07 cm [Lb = 0.07 cm], a diminutive size that reflects the limited yolk reserves available during embryonic development. As the veliger larva transitions to a benthic existence, settlement onto suitable substrate occurs when the shell reaches approximately 0.071 cm , a critical threshold marking the shift from a planktonic to a crawling lifestyle. During this early post-settlement phase, the juvenile snail begins grazing on periphyton and detritus, initiating rapid somatic growth. The species exhibits a relatively modest ultimate shell height of 0.487 cm [Li = 0.487 cm], which is consistent with the small adult body sizes observed across the Valvata genus. Field surveys suggest that adults rarely exceed this dimension, even under favorable conditions in alkaline spring systems, where calcium carbonate availability is typically high.

Sexual maturation in Valvata utahensis is attained when individuals reach a shell height of 0.2475 cm [Lp = 0.2475 cm], a size at which gonadal development and gametogenesis are initiated. This value, derived from observations on the congener Valvata cristata, aligns well with the general pattern among valvatid snails, where puberty occurs at roughly half the ultimate shell height. The attainment of this developmental milestone marks the onset of reproductive competence, though actual spawning may be delayed until favorable environmental cues, such as temperature and food availability, are met. Following puberty, individuals enter a phase of heightened energetic investment in gamete production. The wet weight of a fully grown adult, including the shell, has been estimated at 0.0297 grams [Wwi = 0.0297 grams], a mass that is consistent with size-corrected allometric relationships derived from related planorbid taxa. This modest body mass imposes constraints on the number of offspring that can be produced during a single reproductive bout and influences the overall energetic budget allocated to reproduction versus somatic maintenance.

Reproductive output in Valvata utahensis has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions. At a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females produce approximately 150.0  offspring over their entire lifetime, a figure that draws on reproductive data from the closely related Valvata piscinalis. This lifetime fecundity reflects the cumulative output of multiple spawning events distributed across the adult lifespan. Individual clutches typically consist of small gelatinous egg masses attached to submerged vegetation or hard substrates, with each mass containing a modest number of embryos. The total reproductive effort is ultimately constrained by the small body size of the adult, which limits both the volume of the reproductive tract and the energy reserves available for vitellogenesis. Under the same thermal regime, individuals allocate resources across successive broods, with the inter-clutch interval likely modulated by temperature-dependent metabolic rates. The observed fecundity at 15 °C positions this species as a moderate-income breeder, reliant on continuous food intake to fuel reproduction rather than on stored reserves.

The lifespan of Valvata utahensis has been documented under controlled aquarium conditions maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], where the maximum recorded longevity reaches 374.0 days [am = 374.0 days]. This relatively short lifespan, typical of small-bodied freshwater gastropods, encompasses a single growing season followed by a period of reproductive activity that spans several months. Survival under field conditions is likely lower than this laboratory maximum, owing to predation pressure from leeches, crayfish, and waterfowl, as well as the risk of desiccation during seasonal drawdowns of the shallow water bodies the species inhabits. The thermal regime at which this longevity was recorded (19 °C [T = 19 °C]) is representative of late spring and early summer water temperatures in the Great Basin, when active feeding and reproduction are at their peak. As water temperatures rise toward 25 °C, metabolic costs increase and may accelerate senescence, further compressing the reproductive window. Conversely, cooler temperatures in early spring may slow development but extend the total duration of the active period, illustrating the strong thermal dependence of life-history traits in this species.

Comparative life-history analyses reveal that Valvata utahensis follows a pattern shared among many small valvatid gastropods, characterized by rapid juvenile growth, early maturation, and a compressed reproductive window. The transition from the larval settlement stage, marked by a shell height of 0.071 cm , to the onset of puberty at 0.2475 cm [Lp = 0.2475 cm] occurs relatively quickly under optimal thermal conditions, reflecting the species' strategy of reaching reproductive age before the onset of seasonal environmental stress. The asymptotic body mass of 0.0297 grams [Wwi = 0.0297 grams] represents an evolutionary trade-off between fecundity and predation risk: larger shells confer greater protection from invertebrate predators but require longer developmental periods and higher calcium demands. At the thermal optimum of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the lifetime fecundity of 150.0  offspring yields an estimated daily reproductive rate that is modest compared to more fecund pulmonate snails, but which is sustainable given the species' limited adult body mass and short lifespan. These composite traits—small size, early maturity, moderate fecundity, and a lifespan of 374.0 days [am = 374.0 days] at 19 °C [T = 19 °C]—collectively define Valvata utahensis as an opportunistic colonizer of ephemeral and stable freshwater habitats alike.
